meta.title: Ubuntu Canarias — Welcoming and integrating migrants in the Canary Islands
meta.description: Ubuntu Canarias supports migrants and their families through their social, employment and community integration process in the Canary Islands.

hero.subtitulo: Ubuntu Canarias supports migrants and their families through their social, employment and community integration process, offering guidance, support and new opportunities to build a future with hope.

acogida.texto: First contact, information and personalised support from day one.

empleo.texto: Career guidance, skills training and access to real opportunities for the future.

apoyo.texto: Listening, emotional support and guidance through personal processes.

mediacion.texto: A bridge between cultures for respectful coexistence and genuine integration.

cierre.titulo: No one arrives alone. No one integrates alone.
cierre.texto: We do it together, with respect and hope.

hero.subtitulo: We believe in dignified, participatory and transformative integration.
hero.descripcion: For us, integration isn't a formality settled with a piece of paper or a contract, but a process built day by day, alongside the person and at their own pace. That's why we combine practical guidance — legal, employment, training — with psychosocial support that recognises what each person brings with them: their history, their capabilities and their right to decide over their own life. We work so that the person who arrives is not simply a recipient of help, but an active protagonist of their own process, and so that the host society is also transformed along the way, learning to see migration as an opportunity rather than a problem to be managed.

historia.parrafo1: Ubuntu Canarias was born from the meeting of people who, from different backgrounds and paths, share one conviction: that welcome and integration are built by standing beside people, not from offices detached from the reality of those who arrive.
historia.parrafo2: The association was formed in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, driven by four founding members, as a direct response to the needs the team witnessed, listened to and worked with over years of social work, employment guidance and psychosocial support for migrants across the archipelago.
historia.parrafo3: We are beginning to build a network with organisations, public bodies and citizens, with a will to grow without ever losing the closeness and listening we were born from.

queHacemos.subtitulo: From first contact to full independence, we offer comprehensive support tailored to each person and each stage of their process, in person or remotely.

orientacion.texto: Information and support on immigration, asylum and international protection, together with assistance in administrative procedures. We listen to each situation before pointing a way forward, so every person understands their real options.

integracion.texto: We support the settling-in process: facilitating access to housing, education, and social and health services, and connecting each person with local associations and neighbourhoods across the Canary Islands.

insercion.texto: We design personalised employment pathways, carry out job prospecting and support active job-seeking, working with companies to facilitate the hiring of migrant people.

formacion.texto: As a complementary activity to our main areas, we run Spanish language courses, digital literacy and pre-employment training, together with workshops on transversal skills that open doors to new opportunities.

acompanamiento.texto: We provide individual and group psychological support, with particular attention to migratory grief, emotional accompaniment and referral to specialised mental health resources when needed.

interculturalidad.texto: We facilitate communication and conflict resolution between people of different cultures, institutions and the host society, and run talks, workshops and campaigns to combat racism and xenophobia.

cta.texto: Write to us and we'll support you from the very first step, in person or remotely.

fines.titulo: Reception, integration and the defence of rights
fines.texto: Ubuntu Canarias is a non-profit association working for the social, legal and employment reception and integration of migrant people and their families in the Canary Islands. We combine legal guidance on immigration, asylum and international protection with psychosocial support, intercultural mediation, employment guidance and community awareness-raising, with the aim of facilitating equal access to rights, resources and opportunities.

noticiaPacto.titulo: The European Migration Pact comes into force in the Canary Islands
noticiaPacto.lead: The Canary Islands are calling on Brussels for fast-track transfer mechanisms to mainland Spain as the new European asylum framework takes effect.
noticiaPacto.parrafo1: The European Pact on Migration and Asylum has applied in the Canary Islands since June 12, 2026. The Canary Islands Government has raised concerns about the border screening procedure, which can last up to six months, and is calling for automatic transfer mechanisms to mainland Spain to prevent the islands from becoming a place of prolonged detention.
noticiaPacto.lista1: Accelerated border procedure: people arriving irregularly can be held for up to 12 initial weeks, extendable by another 12 weeks in certain cases.
noticiaPacto.lista2: Faster returns: expulsion is streamlined for those without a right to asylum. Detention periods are extended and return procedures of up to three months are allowed for nationals of countries with asylum acceptance rates below 20%.
noticiaPacto.lista3: Limited transfers: the Pact does not guarantee automatic transfers to mainland Spain. The solidarity mechanism is voluntary, and several member states have said they will contribute only financially, not through relocations.
noticiaPacto.parrafo2: Vice President Octavio Caraballo has said in Brussels that the agreement "must give a voice to border regions" and that, without fast-track transfer mechanisms, "it will not be effective" for the archipelago. President Fernando Clavijo has warned that the impact on border areas could push "rights into the background."
noticiaPacto.parrafo2b: The Canary Islands and the Basque Country have held sessions with NGOs and organisations working with migrants to analyse the consequences of the new framework, which directly affects both regions.
noticiaPacto.efecto1: The average stay in reception centres could rise from one month to as much as six months in some cases.
noticiaPacto.efecto2: Asylum and expulsion processes are being accelerated without clear guarantees of transfer to mainland Spain, increasing the need for legal support throughout the process.
noticiaPacto.efecto3: People in an irregular situation from countries with low asylum recognition rates face a higher risk of rapid deportation.
noticiaPacto.parrafo4: Ubuntu Canarias informs and supports migrants in understanding their rights under the new European framework. If you need guidance on the Pact or your legal situation, get in touch with us.

noticiaCompass.titulo: Ubuntu Canarias joins the COMPASS Collaboration Network
noticiaCompass.lead: A further step toward humane, coordinated and sustainable management of mobility between West Africa and the Canary Islands.
noticiaCompass.parrafo1: We are pleased to announce that Ubuntu Canarias has been officially admitted as a collaborating entity of the COMPASS Collaboration Network, an initiative that brings together institutions, social organisations, universities, businesses and other actors committed to improving the management of human mobility between West Africa and the Canary Islands.
noticiaCompass.parrafo2: Our membership has been approved as part of the COMPASS project – Observatory of Human Mobility between the Canary Islands and Africa, co-financed by the Interreg MAC 2021-2027 Territorial Cooperation Programme.
noticiaCompass.parrafo3: The COMPASS project aims to promote innovative and sustainable solutions to address the challenges of human mobility across the cooperation area formed by the Canary Islands, Gambia, Mauritania and Senegal, encouraging joint work among the different actors involved.
noticiaCompass.listaTitulo: Its main lines of action include:
noticiaCompass.lista1: Promoting international cooperation between public and private entities.
noticiaCompass.lista2: Identifying good practices and needs in the management of human mobility.
noticiaCompass.lista3: Fostering the exchange of knowledge and experience.
noticiaCompass.lista4: Designing strategies that help protect the lives of migrants and strengthen host communities.
noticiaCompass.parrafo4: For Ubuntu Canarias, being part of this network is significant recognition of our commitment to reception, inclusion and social integration. It will also allow us to work with other organisations to develop initiatives that promote a fairer, more supportive and more inclusive society.
noticiaCompass.parrafo5: We continue working to build bridges between people, cultures and institutions, convinced that cooperation is an essential tool for addressing today's and tomorrow's social challenges.
noticiaCompass.parrafo6: Thank you to everyone who trusts in our work. This is only the beginning of a path full of new alliances and opportunities to make a positive impact in the Canary Islands.

blogPrimeraCita.titulo: What to expect at your first guidance appointment
blogPrimeraCita.intro: Taking the first step isn't easy, and it's normal to arrive with questions. This guide sums up how that first meeting with our team works, so you know what to expect and can come in feeling calmer.
blogPrimeraCita.seccion1Texto: It all starts with a first contact: through the website form, choosing "First reception" or "Guidance" as the reason. From there, someone from our team gets in touch with you to arrange the day and format of the meeting, whether in person or by phone, depending on your situation and availability.
blogPrimeraCita.seccion2Texto: You don't need everything sorted or complete to come. If you have any documents related to your situation (identification, paperwork from your administrative process, previous appointments, notifications you've received...), bring them along: it helps us understand your case better. If you don't have anything on hand, that's fine too — what matters is that you come and tell us about your situation in your own words.
blogPrimeraCita.seccion3Texto: The first appointment is, above all, about listening. Our team asks about your current situation, your journey so far, and what you need right now: information, paperwork, employment, training, or psychosocial support. It's not about rushing through a form, but about understanding your specific case before suggesting any path forward.
blogPrimeraCita.seccion4Texto: With that information, we explain the real options available to you and, if appropriate, refer you to the area of the association that best matches your needs: legal and paperwork guidance, job placement, training, interculturality, or psychosocial support. In most cases we set up ongoing follow-up, so it isn't a one-off contact but support throughout the process.
blogPrimeraCita.seccion5Titulo: Before you come, keep in mind
blogPrimeraCita.seccion5Texto: Every situation is different, and the steps can vary from person to person. If you have specific questions before your appointment — what to bring, how to get there, or what to expect in your particular case — write to us and we'll confirm it in advance.

blogAcompanamiento.lead: Why listening before guiding makes a difference in integration processes.
blogAcompanamiento.intro: Throughout my professional career, I've listened to many people who arrive carrying a story with them. And if I've learned one thing in all this time, it's this: before telling someone what to do, you have to understand what has happened to them.
blogAcompanamiento.intro2: It sounds obvious. It isn't. When we set up Ubuntu Canarias, I did it with exactly this in mind: that the first gesture wouldn't be a form, but a listening ear.
blogAcompanamiento.seccion1Texto1: I see it constantly: people who arrive expecting to leave the appointment with a list of steps to follow. And yes, that list does come, at some point. But something else has to happen first.
blogAcompanamiento.seccion1Texto2: That person needs to be able to tell, in their own words and at their own pace, where they've come from and what they've left behind. We shouldn't interrupt them to fill in a box. They need to feel that what they're saying matters before we tell them which papers they need.
blogAcompanamiento.seccion1Texto3: That's not a luxury or a matter of "good manners". It's simply what makes the support that follows actually work.
blogAcompanamiento.seccion2Titulo: What changes when you listen first
blogAcompanamiento.seccion2Texto1: When you truly understand someone's situation — not just their file, but their story — referrals stop being generic. You know whether that person needs reassurance first and paperwork later, or the other way round. You know whether behind a question about employment there's actually a different, more urgent need they haven't dared name yet.
blogAcompanamiento.seccion2Texto2: This is something I'm seeing confirmed right now, almost in real time. We've only just started — we're still operating tentatively, taking our first steps — but I already see it with every person who walks through the door: we don't work with "cases", we work with people, and each one arrives with their own timing. Forcing that timing, going faster than the person can go, doesn't help: it breaks trust exactly when it's needed most.
blogAcompanamiento.seccion3Titulo: Support means holding, not just solving
blogAcompanamiento.seccion3Texto1: There's a difference between resolving a piece of paperwork and supporting a process. The first is closed in a day. The second can take months, sometimes years, and it isn't always a straight line: there are steps forward, steps back, moments when the person simply needs to know we're still there.
blogAcompanamiento.seccion3Texto2: That's why at Ubuntu Canarias we insist so much on follow-up. We don't want to be a one-off contact in anyone's life. We want to be the people you can call again.
blogAcompanamiento.cierreTexto: If there's one thing I'd ask of anyone reading this — whether you need help or you want to offer it — it's the same thing I ask of my team every day: listen a little more before answering.
blogAcompanamiento.firma: — Soraya Mohamedi Mohamed, President of Ubuntu Canarias

blogCulpa.titulo: Why do I feel guilty for having emigrated?
blogCulpa.cabecera: Soraya Mohamedi Mohamed · Psychologist, specialist in Migration and Social Inclusion · Founder and chair of Ubuntu Canarias
blogCulpa.lead: A person holds their phone while looking at a family photograph. On the other side of the screen, a video call with those who stayed in the home country. Sometimes distance is measured in kilometres. Other times, in moments that will never come back.
blogCulpa.seccion1Titulo: There's a question many people ask themselves in silence
blogCulpa.seccion1Texto1: Emigrating is usually associated with the search for opportunities, safety or a better life. But there's a part of that experience that gets talked about far less: guilt.
blogCulpa.seccion1Texto2: Not guilt for having done something wrong. Rather the feeling of having left important people behind right when they might need you too. Sometimes it appears after a phone call. Other times, when news arrives that would have been different had you been there. And sometimes it settles in for no clear reason, like background noise that lingers for months.
blogCulpa.seccion1Texto3: Not every migrant feels it. And those who do don't feel it in the same way. But it's a more common feeling than it seems.
blogCulpa.seccion2Titulo: Life goes on in both places
blogCulpa.seccion2Texto1: While you try to adapt to a new city, find work or sort out paperwork, life carries on in the place you came from.
blogCulpa.seccion2Linea3: Your friends change jobs, start a family, or move away.
blogCulpa.seccion2Texto2: All of that happens even if you talk to them every week.
blogCulpa.seccion2Texto3: There are moments when the distance weighs especially heavily, because it can't be solved with a call or a message.
blogCulpa.seccion3Titulo: Sometimes guilt isn't born from what you do, but from what you can't do
blogCulpa.seccion3Texto1: Many people say the hardest part wasn't leaving. It was discovering they could no longer be there when someone fell ill, needed help, or simply wanted to share an important moment.
blogCulpa.seccion3Texto2: From here, people try to make up for that absence in many ways.
blogCulpa.seccion3Linea3: People try to sound reassuring, even when they don't feel it themselves.
blogCulpa.seccion3Texto3: Without realising it, some people end up living with the feeling that they're always in debt to those who stayed behind.
blogCulpa.seccion4Titulo: There's also guilt for being okay
blogCulpa.seccion4Texto1: This aspect tends to be surprising.
blogCulpa.seccion4Texto2: Some people manage to settle in, find work, or start feeling better in the host country, and it's precisely then that another form of guilt appears.
blogCulpa.seccion4Texto3: Enjoying an opportunity can feel uncomfortable when you know that people you love are still going through hard times.
blogCulpa.seccion4Texto4: It's as if part of you thinks you have no right to feel relief while others keep waiting.
blogCulpa.seccion4Texto5: It doesn't always happen, but when it does, it can cause a lot of confusion.
blogCulpa.seccion5Titulo: Social media changes how distance is experienced
blogCulpa.seccion5Texto1: Years ago it was normal to hear from family every so often. Today it's possible to see almost everything in real time.
blogCulpa.seccion5Linea3: An old photograph someone decides to share.
blogCulpa.seccion5Texto2: That can make distance feel different. Not because there's more separation than before, but because now we witness so many moments we can't be part of.
blogCulpa.seccion6Titulo: There isn't always a perfect decision
blogCulpa.seccion6Texto1: Migration is often framed as a simple choice: stay or leave.
blogCulpa.seccion6Texto2: However, reality tends to be far more complex.
blogCulpa.seccion6Texto3: Some people emigrate because they feel they have no other option. Others do it thinking of their children's future. Some leave planning to return soon and discover the years pass much faster than they imagined.
blogCulpa.seccion6Texto4: Looking back with the information we have today is often unfair. The decision was made with the circumstances of that moment, not those of now.
blogCulpa.seccion7Titulo: An example, to understand it better
blogCulpa.seccion7Texto1: Let's imagine, purely as a hypothetical example, a man who emigrated four years ago. His mother starts having health problems and he can't travel as often as he'd like.
blogCulpa.seccion7Texto2: Every time he speaks to her, he feels he should be there. At the same time, he knows going back would mean losing the job it took him so much effort to get.
blogCulpa.seccion7Texto4: And that's exactly why guilt appears: because any decision means giving something up.
blogCulpa.seccion8Texto1: There's no way to stop feeling guilty overnight.
blogCulpa.seccion8Texto2: Some people find it helps to understand that loving their family and building a life in another country aren't two incompatible things.
blogCulpa.seccion8Texto3: Others discover that talking openly about that feeling, instead of hiding it, lightens some of the weight they'd been carrying.
blogCulpa.seccion8Texto4: It can also help to remember that distance doesn't measure commitment or love. Some people are very present while living thousands of kilometres away, and others live nearby yet are barely part of their family's life.
blogCulpa.seccion8Texto5: Every migration story has its own nuances. Comparing it to someone else's rarely helps.
blogCulpa.seccion9Texto1: Over time I've learned that many migrants miss more than just a place. They also miss the chance to be where they feel they should have been at certain moments.
blogCulpa.seccion9Texto2: Perhaps that's why guilt appears so easily.
blogCulpa.seccion9Texto3: It doesn't always go away completely. But once it's named, it stops being a confusing feeling and starts to be understood as part of a deeply human experience.
blogCulpa.seccion9Texto4: And perhaps that understanding won't close the distance, but it can help you look at yourself with a little more kindness.
blogCulpa.seccion10Titulo: When guilt takes up too much space
blogCulpa.seccion10Texto1: Guilt doesn't usually disappear because someone tells us we shouldn't feel it. Sometimes it needs time. Other times, it needs us to stop trying to hide it or play it down.
blogCulpa.seccion10Texto2: Some people find it helps to talk about it with someone they trust, without feeling obliged to pretend everything is fine. Others find relief when they accept that they can't be present for every important moment in their family's life, and that this limitation doesn't lessen the love they feel for them.
blogCulpa.seccion10Texto3: It can also help to set aside space to look after the life being built here. Allowing yourself to enjoy good news, make new friends, or feel at peace in the host country doesn't mean forgetting the place you came from or the people who stayed there. Both things can coexist, even if it's hard to believe at first.
blogCulpa.seccion10Texto4: Every migration process is different, and there's no single correct way to live it. Some people need to talk a lot about what they left behind, while others prefer to do so little by little. What matters isn't following a specific path, but finding a way to move forward without letting guilt take up all the space.
blogCulpa.seccion10Texto5: If, over time, this feeling becomes constant, gets in the way of rest, affects relationships, or means every moment of wellbeing comes with remorse, seeking professional support can be an option. Not because feeling guilty is a problem in itself, but because no one has to face what's causing them pain alone.
blogCulpa.cierre: Soraya Mohamedi Mohamed · Psychologist, specialist in Migration and Social Inclusion

blogMarMuro.titulo: When the sea stops being a wall
blogMarMuro.cabecera: Soraya Mohamedi Mohamed · Psychologist, specialist in Migration and Social Inclusion · Founder and chair of Ubuntu Canarias
blogMarMuro.lead: A Supreme Court ruling limits summary pushbacks for people who cross by swimming. It coincides with a surge in crossings in Ceuta. What the ruling says, what it doesn't explain, and why it's worth looking beyond the coincidence.
blogMarMuro.intro: On 8 July, Spain's Supreme Court confirmed something that might look like a technicality but actually carries very concrete consequences: people intercepted at sea while trying to swim into Ceuta or Melilla cannot be subjected to a summary pushback.
blogMarMuro.seccion1Texto1: Spanish immigration law allows what's known as "border rejection" — immediate expulsion, without individual identification or legal assistance — for anyone who crosses a physical containment barrier, such as a fence. The Supreme Court has established that the sea does not fall into that category. There is nothing material to "cross" in the water, so anyone intercepted while swimming must be subject to the ordinary return procedure, which carries more safeguards: a prior hearing, a reasoned decision and judicial review.
blogMarMuro.seccion1Texto2: It's a ruling that sets binding case law. There is no appeal against it.
blogMarMuro.seccion2Titulo: Less than ten kilometres, several hours of darkness
blogMarMuro.seccion2Texto1: Between Fnideq (Castillejos) and Ceuta there are less than ten kilometres in a straight line, at the narrowest point of the strait. On paper, that sounds like little. In the water, at night, with no boat and no professional support, it's something else entirely.
blogMarMuro.seccion2Texto2: Accounts from people who have made it describe three to four hours of continuous swimming, with no rest, through fog, wind and swell, guided only by the lights of the Ceuta coastline. Not everyone makes it. In recent days, several bodies have been recovered from the waters off Ceuta of people who did not complete the crossing.
blogMarMuro.seccion2Texto3: The land border fence, six metres high with a double structure, has become almost impossible to cross. That's why more and more people are choosing the sea: not because it's easier, but because they believe it gives them more of a chance.
blogMarMuro.seccion3Titulo: What has happened since the ruling
blogMarMuro.seccion3Texto1: In recent weeks, Ceuta has seen a notable surge in crossings: between 1,500 and 2,000 people entered irregularly in barely ten days, most of them by swimming. The president of the autonomous city has spoken of a humanitarian emergency. The Civil Guard, through its professional association, has warned of a possible "pull effect" and has called for clear protocols in what it describes as an operational vacuum.
blogMarMuro.seccion3Texto2: It's tempting — and understandable — to weave these two facts into a single story: the ruling would have opened a door, and thousands of people would be walking through it. But that reading calls for caution. Two things happening in the same period of time doesn't automatically mean one caused the other. Migrants' decisions rarely respond to a single factor, and even less to a court ruling that most people probably don't even know about in any detail.
blogMarMuro.seccion3Texto3: Someone who decides to get into the water for three or four hours of swimming isn't doing it because of a legal technicality. They do it after having exhausted other routes, carrying the accumulated exhaustion of previous attempts, and working with information that arrives in fragments, sometimes distorted by those who profit from selling the crossing as safer than it is.
blogMarMuro.seccion4Titulo: The question that's actually worth asking
blogMarMuro.seccion4Texto1: Beyond its immediate effects, what this ruling brings into view is an underlying tension that runs through the whole of current European migration policy. The European Pact on Migration and Asylum, in force since June this year, is moving toward a model centred on border control and faster return procedures. The Supreme Court's ruling, by contrast, moves in the opposite direction: it expands safeguards rather than reducing them.
blogMarMuro.seccion4Texto2: That contradiction isn't a problem of the court or of European law taken separately. It reflects a system that still hasn't resolved what role it wants to give individual rights when set against border management as a security issue. And that lack of definition is paid for, almost always, in the bodies of the people who cross.
blogMarMuro.seccion5Texto1: Behind every figure like "1,500 people in ten days" are decisions made under a kind of pressure most of us will never fully grasp: three hours swimming in the dark, the exhaustion of previous attempts, incomplete information, the calculation of a risk that no ruling can reduce. Understanding that context doesn't exempt institutions from legislating responsibly. But it should push us, before jumping to conclusions about cause and effect, to look more carefully at what lies behind each crossing.
blogMarMuro.cierre: — Soraya Mohamedi Mohamed · Psychologist, specialist in Migration and Social Inclusion

blogHomologacion.titulo: Getting a foreign qualification recognised in Spain: what no one explains at the start
blogHomologacion.lead: Someone who worked as a nurse for ten years back home, or who holds a master's degree in engineering, arrives here and runs into an uncomfortable question: is that qualification worth anything, or do you have to start from zero? The short answer is “it depends”, and that short answer is exactly what causes the most anxiety, because no one explains well what it depends on.
blogHomologacion.s1Titulo: Four procedures that get confused under the same word
blogHomologacion.s1Texto: “Homologación” (recognition) has become the catch-all term for “making my qualification count here”, but there are actually four different procedures, and mixing them up wastes time and, sometimes, money on the wrong one.
blogHomologacion.tablaHtml:
ProcedureWhat it's forWho it's forWhere to applyKey requirements
Homologación (recognition)Makes your foreign qualification equivalent to a Spanish one so you can practise a regulated professionGraduates in medicine, education, engineering, law…Electronic office of the Ministry of Science, Innovation and UniversitiesLegalised, apostilled and translated qualification, academic transcript and proof of fee payment, mainly
Equivalencia (equivalence)Recognises the academic level of your official bachelor's or master's degree, without linking it to a regulated professionGraduates who don't need to practise regulated professionsElectronic office of the same Ministry (or a university, for a doctorate)The same documents as homologación
Convalidación (course credit transfer)Recognises subjects or credits already completedStudents who want to continue their studies at a Spanish universityThe Spanish university where you want to studyAcademic transcript and course syllabi; subject to each university's own deadlines and fees
Reconocimiento (EU recognition)Allows you to practise a regulated profession in Spain if the qualification was obtained in the EUEU citizens in regulated professionsThe competent Ministry for that profession (Health, Education, etc.)Official qualification and profession-specific documentation
blogHomologacion.s2Titulo: The question to ask before starting any procedure
blogHomologacion.s2Texto:
It's not “can I get my qualification recognised?”, it's “do I actually need it recognised for what I want to do?”. That's where many people lose months.

One fact that surprises many people: you don't need a work permit in Spain, or even to be living here, to start the recognition procedure. If the qualification is official in your home country, you can start the process from abroad, even before migrating.

On the other hand, not everything can be recognised. Continuing-education diplomas, qualifications that aren't an official bachelor's or master's degree, ones that already received a negative decision, and those obtained mainly through recognition of work experience rather than formal study are all excluded. And if you're already processing a convalidación of those studies directly with a Spanish university, you don't also need to go through homologación — the two don't combine.

If your goal is to work in a regulated profession — teaching at a public school, practising medicine, nursing, law — you do need full homologación, no shortcuts. If your goal is a non-regulated job, it's often better to start job-hunting with the unrecognised qualification, explaining it clearly at interview, and leave the recognition process running in parallel rather than treating it as a prerequisite. Waiting for the qualification to be recognised before job-hunting, when the job doesn't actually require it, is one of the most common and most time-costly mistakes.
blogHomologacion.s3Texto:
Not every degree requires the long procedure. Regulated professions — the ones that require homologación if the qualification is from outside the EU — are concentrated in a few specific sectors: health (medicine, nursing, physiotherapy, dentistry, pharmacy, health psychology, among others), higher and technical engineering and architecture, teaching (from early years through vocational training), and the legal field (lawyers and court representatives). This list is set out in the annex to Royal Decree 889/2022.

One important nuance for anyone coming from abroad with a law degree: for the legal profession, getting the qualification recognised isn't the last step. Afterwards you still need to complete the Master's in Access to the Legal Profession and pass the corresponding state exam before you can practise.
blogHomologacion.s4Titulo: If what you want recognised isn't a university degree
blogHomologacion.s4Texto:
Everything above — the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities, the €166.50 fee — applies to bachelor's, master's or other degree-level qualifications. If what you completed in your home country was secondary education or the equivalent of A-levels/high school, the procedure is handled by the Ministry of Education, Vocational Training and Sport, with general information on its official website.

If it's specifically a Vocational Training (FP) qualification, and the goal is to access FP studies in Spain by presenting that foreign qualification, it needs to be recognised first through that same Ministry's electronic office. For any doubts about the procedure, the Ministry runs its own citizen support service.

If you live in the Canary Islands, there's also a separate procedure run by the Government of the Canary Islands for recognising the equivalence of a qualification or completed studies, when that equivalence needs an individual decision. Unlike university homologación, this procedure has no fee, can be submitted year-round, and allows two routes:

  • Online, with the application form, ID document and academic qualification or transcript.
  • In person, at any registry office of the Government of the Canary Islands, with the same documents.

One important clarification: this recognition gives the same academic or professional effects as the qualification it's compared to, but does not grant the Spanish qualification itself.
blogHomologacion.s5Titulo: What the university procedure actually asks for
blogHomologacion.s5Texto:
Since November 2022, recognition of foreign university qualifications is handled exclusively through the electronic office of the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities. It isn't done on paper, and it isn't done over the counter.

The documents you need to upload, with their exact name in the system:

  • IDENTIDAD — your ID document (usually a passport).
  • TITULO — the original qualification, legalised or apostilled if applicable.
  • TRADTITULO — a certified translation of the qualification, if it isn't in Spanish.
  • CAO — the official academic transcript (subjects completed), or the Diploma Supplement if you have one instead.
  • TRADCAO — a certified translation of that transcript, if it isn't in Spanish.
  • LINGU — proof of Spanish level, required only for homologación (not for equivalencia).
  • TASA — proof of fee payment.

On legalising the original qualification, there are two valid routes: through the education authorities of the country where it was obtained, or through the Spanish consular office in that same country. Either one works.

A practical detail: although the technical limit is 10 MB per file, it's best not to go over 5 MB, to avoid upload problems.

The fee costs €166.50 and can be paid in four ways: with form 790 printed and paid at a Spanish bank, by transfer to a Bank of Spain account enabled for payments from abroad, online by card or account, or waived if you're a beneficiary of temporary protection.

On access: you need to identify yourself with Cl@ve (if you have a NIF or NIE) or, if you don't have those, create a user account with your passport or other documentation from your home country. A curious detail: if the system throws an error when creating the account because the passport number “matches the format” of a NIF or NIE, simply adding three zeros before the number avoids the conflict.

The application can be saved as a draft and picked up again later — although uploaded documents aren't kept between sessions, only the written data is — so it's worth having everything gathered before sitting down to fill it in completely.
blogHomologacion.s6Titulo: What almost no one mentions: the wait isn't just bureaucratic, it's emotional
blogHomologacion.s6Texto:
Waiting more than a year for an answer on whether your training “counts” here isn't just a slow procedure. For many people it touches directly on professional identity: years of study and experience are left in a kind of limbo, with no one — not the system, and sometimes not even the person themselves — quite sure what to do with them in the meantime. There's no way to speed this up that doesn't depend on the administration, and pretending there's a magic shortcut doesn't help anyone.

The law sets a 6-month deadline to resolve applications, but in practice it's common for it to take considerably longer. The more complete and clear the documentation from the start, the fewer reasons the administration will have to request clarifications that delay the process further.

If the decision ends up being unfavourable, it isn't the end of the road: you can file a complaint with the Ministry itself within one month of notification, and if that complaint doesn't succeed either, there's an appeal to the administrative courts. It's not a path anyone would choose, but it exists.

What does help is not putting life on hold while you wait. Working in something else during that time isn't a failure or a step backwards — it's simply what needs to be done while a procedure moves at its own pace, which is almost never the pace you'd want.
blogHomologacion.s7Titulo: What the official channels don't tell you: the community does
blogHomologacion.s7Texto:
There's something telling in all this: not even the Ministry of Universities publishes data on how long recognitions actually take. What's known about real waiting times comes almost always from the people going through the process themselves, sharing it with each other.

During review, you may receive a requerimiento — a request for additional documentation the Ministry considers necessary. From the moment it's received, you have 10 working days to respond, with the possibility of requesting an extension if you need more time. Failing to sort it out in time can lead to the file being closed, although if that happens because a notification never arrived, you can file an appeal explaining it.

It's also common, especially in health professions, for them to ask for a certificate of continuous professional practice if six years or more have passed since the qualification was obtained — a document certifying your work experience, which also needs to be legalised and apostilled like the rest.

Since the Ministry doesn't provide this information officially, citizen communities and platforms have formed, made up of people going through the recognition process, where real waiting times, questions and concrete experiences are shared. They don't replace official information, but for day-to-day questions about the procedure they're often more useful than any institutional website.
blogHomologacion.fuentesHtml:
• Recognition of university qualifications — Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities: universidades.sede.gob.es
  • Declaration of academic-level equivalence — Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities: universidades.sede.gob.es
  • Recognition of non-university studies (secondary/high school) — Ministry of Education, Vocational Training and Sport: educacionfpydeportes.gob.es
  • Recognition of Vocational Training (FP) qualifications — Ministry of Education, Vocational Training and Sport: educacionyfp.gob.es
  • Equivalence of non-university studies in the Canary Islands (no fee) — Government of the Canary Islands: sede.gobiernodecanarias.org — procedure 5862
blogHomologacion.recursosTexto: Besides the official sources, there are citizen-run platforms created by people who have been through the recognition process, where experiences, real waiting times and frequently asked questions are shared: homologacionjustaya.org. It isn't an official source, but it can be useful for day-to-day questions the administration doesn't always answer.
